web_title: 9. Both Sides of the Aisle, Likely Outcomes & Capital Preservation Plan
book_title: Both Sides of the Aisle: Bull vs. Bear Steelman, Expected Value & Why We Reject at Current Prices
question: Why does McKesson move from ACCUMULATE_ON_DIP (TIER_1) to REJECTED (TIER_0, VALUATION) despite its COMPOUNDER_PASS business quality, and what exact conditions would bring it back?

epigraph.quote: Saying no to a great company at the wrong price-to-risk ratio is how permanent capital stays intact.
epigraph.author: Portfolio Synthesis Rule

web_blocks.title: Both Sides of the Aisle: Bull vs. Bear Steelman

web_blocks.html: This side-by-side steelman weighs McKesson's oligopoly compounding engine against the valuation, governance, legal, and concentration headwinds that emerged in our Pass 2 audit.

web_blocks.caption: Institutional Steelman: Bull Thesis vs. Bear Thesis
headers: Bear Case Steelman (Why We Reject Here)
rows: 90%+ U.S. drug distribution moat; Oncology & Multispecialty (2.96% margin) + RxTS (19.45% margin) + PMG/Core Ventures lift profit pools [2, 6, 14, 19].
Core gross margin compressed to 3.49%–3.61%; GLP-1s dilute percentage margins while Medical-Surgical Q2 FY27 Adj. OP fell 10% YoY [2, 8, 25].
Strong $5.41B FY26 FCF (106% conversion) and $6.53B Q2 FY27 cash fund buybacks and M&A while maintaining investment-grade liquidity [2, 3].
$15.22B senior claims ($5.55B net debt/obligations incl. $3,234M Med-Surg term loan + $5.16B opioid + $2.56B NCI + $1.95B leases) against -$3,954M equity deficit [3, 21].
CVS Health contract extended through June 2032, locking in multi-year volume visibility [2, 6].
CVS concentration (~24% FY26 rev, rising toward ~32% rev / ~38% AR), Nov 16 CEO Brian Tyler retirement, Nov 19 DOJ/FTC scrutiny, and O'Connor cyber class actions [1, 3].
FY27E Adj. EPS guidance $45.60–$46.40 (+17%–19% YoY) and 76.71% ROIC support top-quartile multiples [6, 25].
$1,160.00 DCF Base (0.45:1 CMP R:R; 1.28:1 even at $994.71 zone low) and Finviz $1,173.21 (0.51:1) fail the 1.50:1 hurdle; 17.25x mid-cycle P/E implies $904.59 [24, 25].
web_blocks.takeaway: McKesson remains an elite operational compounder, but $15.22B in senior claims, governance/regulatory overhangs, and sub-1.50:1 asymmetry force a REJECTED (VALUATION) call.

web_blocks.html: We raise Bear probability from 20% to 25% for CEO transition risk, DOJ/FTC scrutiny, O'Connor litigation, and multiple compression. That lowers Expected Value to $1,113.00 (+4.1% from $1,069.43).

web_blocks.html: Re-Underwriting Upgrade Trigger: Re-evaluate MCK from REJECTED only if shares pull back below $980.00 (offering >=1.50:1 R:R to $1,160.00 against $865.85 stop) OR if post-Wellverse Form 10 disclosures and CEO transition clarity lift DCF Base fair value above $1,250.00.

Structural Break Trigger: Keep MCK on permanent pass if weekly closes break below $865.85 on heavy volume, DOJ/FTC scrutiny restricts specialty M&A, or CVS Health contract economics compress North American Pharma margins.

MCK is REJECTED (TIER_0, VALUATION) and NOT_HELD (0 shares), so 100% of capital stays in Cash / T-Bills. Shortlist peer AbbVie (ABBV) trades at $287.68 (17.61x forward P/E) with 0.63:1 CMP R:R to $310.00 against its $252.23 stop. Outside candidate Costco (COST) trades at $1,094.01 (43.50x forward P/E) with 0.44:1 CMP R:R to $1,150.00 against its $966.03 stop. Neither clears our 1.50:1 hurdle, so both receive 0%.

Our thesis rests on one falsifiable hinge. McKesson must sustain 10.5%+ EBIT growth and 3.5%/yr share shrinkage through FY2029E without CVS concessions, IRA Part B / 340B fee pressure, or DOJ/FTC delays [3, 4, 20]. Until price drops below $980.00 or Base fair value tops $1,250.00, 100% cash remains optimal.

Our capital preservation plan stays disciplined during the S&P 500 Downtrend (38.8% above 50DMA, 10 distribution days) [24]. We hold 0 shares of MCK and decline the $18,365 LEAPS call. Both AbbVie (ABBV) and Costco (COST) remain at 0% allocation until cleaner 1.50:1 setups emerge.

book_paragraphs: Every great company has a price at which the risk-reward stops working. Our Pass 2 re-underwriting moves McKesson from ACCUMULATE_ON_DIP (TIER_1) to REJECTED (TIER_0, VALUATION). The business still earns COMPOUNDER_PASS—it runs an irreplaceable 90%+ oligopoly toll road—but the stock at $1,069.43 offers only 0.45-to-1 reward-to-risk to our $1,160.00 DCF Base, and even the $994.71 support zone low delivers just 1.28-to-1 [24].

New risks discovered in the November 2026 filings reinforce that discipline. Beyond $15.22 billion in senior claims, investors now face CEO Brian Tyler's November 16 retirement transition, November 19 DOJ/FTC scrutiny, the O'Connor cybersecurity class actions, and rising CVS Health concentration [3]. Raising Bear probability to 25% drops probability-weighted Expected Value to $1,113.00, just +4.1% above the November 20 close.

We hold 0 shares (NOT_HELD), keep 100% of earmarked capital in cash, and decline the $18,365 LEAPS call (24.45% of NAV). Patience will either deliver a sub-$980 entry with genuine 1.50:1 asymmetry or protect our cash for cleaner setups.

Every investment committee must answer two questions at the end of an audit: what could make us wrong, and where should the money go instead? On the Bull side, McKesson's 90%+ distribution oligopoly, 76.71% ROIC, and 17% to 19% FY2027E Adjusted EPS growth ($45.60 to $46.40) give it rare earnings visibility [2, 6, 25]. Its CVS Health contract runs through June 2032, and Oncology plus RxTS continue to expand consolidated profit pools [2, 6].

On the Bear side, four concrete risks argue against paying 20x forward earnings today. First, CVS Health concentration sits at 24% of FY2026 revenue and trends toward 32% of revenue and 38% of trade receivables on contract mix, while top-10 suppliers represent 71% of purchases [1]. Second, total senior claims of $15.22 billion—including $3,234 million of Med-Surg term loans, $5.16 billion of opioid liabilities, $2.56 billion of redeemable NCI, and $1.95 billion of leases—sit ahead of -$3,954 million in stockholders' deficit [3]. Third, CEO Brian Tyler's November 16 retirement announcement, November 19 DOJ/FTC scrutiny, and O'Connor cybersecurity class actions (3:26-cv-02929-L) create real execution and legal overhang [3]. Fourth, 2027–2028 IRA Medicare Part B and 340B policy shifts could pressure specialty margins [4, 20].

Weighting those scenarios at 20% Bull ($1,350.00), 55% Base ($1,160.00), and 25% Bear ($820.00) yields an Expected Value of $1,113.00—just +4.1% above the $1,069.43 close. Because neither CMP (0.45:1) nor the $994.71 support zone low (1.28:1) clears our 1.50:1 hurdle, we assign REJECTED (TIER_0, VALUATION), keep 100% of capital in cash, decline the $18,365 LEAPS call, and wait for either a sub-$980.00 reset or a fundamental fair-value step-up above $1,250.00.

Good investing requires holding two opposing ideas in mind without flinching. On the Bull side, McKesson is an entrenched healthcare utility that has compounded free cash flow and shrunk its share count relentlessly for a decade [2, 16]. Its Oncology & Multispecialty segment and Prescription Technology Solutions business give it higher-margin growth engines that legacy wholesalers struggle to match [2, 6].

On the Bear side, four overlapping risks make the current valuation unforgiving. First, customer concentration in CVS Health sits at 24% of FY2026 revenue and trends toward 32% of revenue and 38% of trade receivables on contract mix, while top-10 suppliers account for 71% of purchases [1]. Second, $15.22 billion of senior claims—including $3,234 million of Med-Surg term loans, $5.16 billion of opioid liabilities, $2.56 billion of redeemable NCI, and $1.95 billion of leases—sit ahead of -$3,954 million in stockholders' deficit [3].

Third, November 2026 brought sharp governance and legal catalysts: CEO Brian Tyler's November 16 retirement announcement, November 19 DOJ/FTC scrutiny around distribution consolidation, and putative cybersecurity class-action lawsuits led by O'Connor v. McKesson Corporation (3:26-cv-02929-L) [3]. Fourth, 2027–2028 IRA Medicare Part B and 340B policy shifts threaten oncology reimbursement spreads [4, 20].

When we weight Bull ($1,350.00 at 20%), Base ($1,160.00 at 55%), and Bear ($820.00 at 25%), probability-weighted Expected Value is $1,113.00—just +4.1% above the $1,069.43 close. Neither CMP (0.45:1 R:R) nor the $994.71 support zone low (1.28:1 R:R) clears our 1.50:1 hurdle. We therefore assign REJECTED (TIER_0, VALUATION), hold 0 shares (NOT_HELD), keep 100% in cash, decline the $18,365 LEAPS call, and assign 0% to both ABBV and COST until cleaner asymmetry appears.

In portfolio management, the hardest discipline is not spotting bad companies; it is saying no to good companies when the odds are stacked against you. McKesson is undeniably a high-quality business. It controls roughly a third of U.S. pharmaceutical distribution inside a three-player oligopoly, converts over 100% of GAAP net income into Free Cash Flow, and holds a long-term CVS Health contract through June 2032 [2, 6, 18].

Yet the same filings that confirm McKesson's operational strength also reveal why new capital cannot chase here. CVS Health concentration stands at 24% of FY2026 revenue and trends toward 32% of revenue and 38% of trade receivables on contract mix, while top-10 suppliers represent 71% of purchases [1]. At the same time, $15.22 billion of senior claims—including $3,234 million of Med-Surg term debt, $5.16 billion of opioid liabilities, $2.56 billion of redeemable NCI, and $1.95 billion of leases—sit ahead of -$3,954 million in stockholders' deficit [3].

November 2026 also introduced three acute governance and legal overhangs: CEO Brian Tyler's November 16 retirement announcement, November 19 DOJ and FTC scrutiny around distribution consolidation, and putative cybersecurity class-action lawsuits led by O'Connor v. McKesson Corporation (3:26-cv-02929-L) [3]. Raising our Bear case probability from 20% to 25% lowers probability-weighted Expected Value to $1,113.00—just +4.1% above the $1,069.43 close.

Because neither CMP (0.45:1 R:R) nor the $994.71 support zone low (1.28:1 R:R) clears our 1.50:1 hurdle against the $865.85 stop, we downgrade MCK from ACCUMULATE_ON_DIP (TIER_1) to REJECTED (TIER_0, VALUATION). We hold 0 shares (NOT_HELD), keep 100% of earmarked capital in cash, decline the $18,365 LEAPS call, and assign 0% to shortlist peer ABBV and outside candidate COST until genuine 1.50:1 asymmetry returns.

We also checked whether capital earmarked for McKesson should rotate immediately into AbbVie (ABBV) or Costco (COST). AbbVie trades at $287.68 (17.61x forward P/E, Stage 2) with support at $278.20–$286.68 and a stop at $252.23, offering 0.63:1 CMP reward-to-risk to $310.00. Costco trades at $1,094.01 (43.50x forward P/E, Stage 2) with support at $1,018.73–$1,081.96 and a stop at $966.03, offering 0.44:1 CMP reward-to-risk to $1,150.00.

Because neither alternative clears our 1.50:1 hurdle at current prices, both receive a 0% allocation. Holding 100% in Cash / T-Bills keeps dry powder intact until the S&P 500 Downtrend (38.8% above 50DMA, 10 distribution days) produces fat-pitch entries with genuine institutional asymmetry [24].

That is the essence of institutional capital preservation. We admire McKesson's 90%+ distribution moat, its -$7.78 billion working-capital flywheel, and its Oncology and RxTS profit engines [2, 18]. Yet at $1,069.43 (0.45:1 CMP R:R) or even $994.71 (1.28:1 zone-low R:R), the odds fail our 1.50:1 mandate. Keeping 100% of capital in Cash / T-Bills—and declining the $18,365 LEAPS call—ensures we only deploy risk when both business quality and price asymmetry align.

Until McKesson either resets below $980.00 with stabilizing 4-hour momentum or demonstrates fundamental fair value above $1,250.00 post-Wellverse separation, our capital remains safely parked in cash with zero equity or options exposure.

In closing, McKesson stays on our high-quality watchlist as a COMPOUNDER_PASS business, while our capital decision remains REJECTED (TIER_0, VALUATION) with 0 shares held, 100% cash preserved, and zero options exposure.

If future market volatility delivers a sub-$980.00 entry with stabilizing momentum or if Wellverse separation unlocks higher sustainable free cash flow, we will re-underwrite McKesson from scratch with fresh eyes and full rigor.
